newsitem.title: ANTIGUA AND BARBUDA: Caribbean leaders prepare for Clinton visit.
newsitem.headline: Caribbean leaders prepare for Clinton visit.

text.p: Jamaica's prime minister said on Friday he hoped a summit meeting in May with President Bill Clinton will put U.S.-Caribbean relations on a firmer footing, following a series of rifts.

"We intend to discuss those matters that are important to the development and security of the region and the preservation of democracy," Jamaican Prime Minister P.J. Patterson said. "We are now preparing a common regional position for the visit with president Clinton."
Clinton's summit with the 14-member Caribbean Community is set for May in Barbados.
In addition to Caricom leaders, the presidents of Haiti and the Dominican Republic have also been invited.

Caribbean leaders have argued that Washington's latest policy moves in the region would serve only to undermine it politically and economically. The end result, they said, would be increased use of the Caribbean as a drug trans-shipment point and increased migration to the US.

Patterson, speaking at the bi-annual Caricom meeting in Antigua, said there was a growing view in Washington that the United States should be "activists and interventionists" in the Caribbean because of the region's tiny economies.

In recent months, the United States has challenged the Caribbean's preferential banana trade with Europe before the World Trade Organisation and has proposed a WTO rule change that would end preferential rum trade several years ahead of schedule.

The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration has crippled regional air carriers by demoting several countries to category II status, thus barring them from adding new flights in a region where American Airlines controls 70 pct of all routes.

The Caribbean also has serious problems with U.S. attempts to tighten an embargo against Cuba. The stricter embargo is seen by regional officials both as an attempt to circumscribe the sovereignty of countries in the region and as a policy that could destabilise Cuba economically, which in turn would have implications for the entire region.

Just two months ago, Washington accused the Jamaican government of knowingly harbouring at least one elected official with drug connections. The United States threatened Jamaica with decertification if it failed to sign a drug interdiction accord that would allow U.S. agents to operate in Jamaican waters and airspace.
